headline: Recommended approval of ethical procurement and short-term rental rules; pay-to-play, condo conversion, AI, and tree rules kept in committee.
summary: The ethical procurement ordinance was recommended 4-1, with Councilor Strezo opposed. The city solicitor and chief procurement officer raised legal and implementation questions about it. Councilors also adopted wording changes to the pay-to-play ordinance, which was kept in committee.
decisions: Accepted the minutes of the October 13, 2026 committee meeting, 5-0.
Adopted the amended text of the ethical procurement ordinance, 4-1.
Recommended approval of the ethical procurement ordinance, 4-1, with Councilor Strezo opposed.
Adopted striking “in their capacity” from Section 15-73(b) of the pay-to-play ordinance, 4-0 with one recusal.
Kept the pay-to-play ordinance amendment in committee.
Kept the tree protection ordinance in committee.
Recommended approval of short-term rental ordinance changes as amended, 5-0.
Kept the condominium conversion amendment in committee.
Kept the Artificial Intelligence Ordinance in committee.

transcript:
## City of Somerville, Massachusetts City Council Legislative Matters Committee Meeting Minutes

Tuesday, October 27, 2026

6:00 PM

- This meeting was held virtually via Zoom and was called to order at 6:00 pm
- by Chair Scott and adjourned at 8:39 pm with a roll call vote of 4 in favor (Councilors Davis, Mbah,

Ewen-Campen and Scott), none opposed, and one absent (Councilor Strezo).

Councilor Strezo arrived at 6:10 pm.

Also present: Colin Zeigler - Director of Public Health, Amanda Nagim-Williams - Director of Intergovernmental Affairs, Brendan Salisbury - Legislative Policy Analyst, Lisa Davidson - Director of Housing, Cindy Amara - City Solicitor, Angela Allen - Chief Procurement Officer, Jason Piques - Assistant City Solicitor and Delaney Fisher-Cassiol - Clerk of Committees

Roll Call

- Present: Ward Six City Councilor Lance L. Davis, City Councilor At
- Large Wilfred N. Mbah, Ward Three City Councilor Ben
- Ewen-Campen, City Councilor At Large Kristen Strezo and
- Ward Two City Councilor Jefferson Thomas (J.T.) Scott

1. Committee

Approval of the Minutes of the Legislative Matters Committee Meeting of Minutes

October 13, 2026.

(ID # 26-1575 )

- RESULT: ACCEPTED
- AYE:

- Ward Six City Councilor Davis, City Councilor At Large
- Mbah, Ward Three City Councilor Ewen-Campen, City
- Councilor At Large Strezo and Ward Two City Councilor
- Scott

2. Ordinance

By Councilor Ewen-Campen, Councilor Wheeler, Councilor Mbah and (ID # 26-1023 ) Councilor Link

- That Chapter 2, Article VIII, Division 1 of the Code of Ordinances be
- amended as detailed within.

Councilor Ewen-Campen reviewed the attachment, Legislative Matters -

**2026-10-27** Ethical Procurement Amendment (with 26-1023), and noted

several amendments developed with city staff, including aligning the language with the city's style guide, removing paragraph titles and definitions, and moving the sole proprietor provision.

Chair Scott moved to adopt the text in the handout Legislative Matters -

**2026-10-27** Ethical Procurement Amendment (with 26-1023). This

motion was adopted on a roll call vote of 4 in favor (Councilors Davis, Mbah, Ewen-Campen and Scott), one opposed (Councilor Strezo), and none absent.

Councilor Strezo described the ordinance as illegal and discriminatory and stated that she would vote against it. In response to her questions about its legality, City Solicitor Cindy Amara explained that the amendments

- primarily clarify the ordinance without changing its underlying legal issues.

In response to a question from Councilor Davis about legal challenges, Solicitor Amara identified potential federal Commerce Clause issues, noting

that certain matters fall under federal authority and that the ordinance might not be upheld without congressional authorization. She also raised questions

about potential discrimination and conflicts with the purpose of procurement. Angela Allen, Chief Procurement Officer, raised practical

implementation concerns, including whether the city has the authority to bar certain bidders or existing contractors, how compliance would be

determined and who would make the final decision. She questioned whether appearing on a list within the past three fiscal years would be sufficient

grounds to deny a bidder and noted that the process could undermine a level playing field.

Councilor Ewen-Campen explained that the intent was for bidders to self-attest to compliance through a checkbox on procurement documents, with the city consulting the list referenced in Section C if there were a

disagreement. He noted that the issue is complex and changes over time, so the city should retain discretion rather than rely exclusively on the list.

- Councilor Davis questioned whether the certification language clearly

established what bidders were required to attest to and expressed concern that the word “consistently” could exclude companies based on gaps in their

activity. Brendan Salisbury, Legislative Policy Analyst, clarified that the list in Section C is a means of assessing whether a company meets the criteria in

- Sections A and B, rather than definitive proof of noncompliance.

- Chair Scott identified implementation and legal challenges as the two
- remaining concerns. He expressed confidence that Chief Procurement

Officer Allen could manage implementation and that the Mayor could execute the law, adding that the possibility of a legal challenge should not

prevent the city from establishing policy. Councilor Davis noted that municipalities are generally restricted from regulating matters already

governed by comprehensive bodies of law and asked whether the city could argue that the ordinance was intended only to govern its own spending.

- Solicitor Amara responded that legal analysis considers the ordinance's

actions and effects, not just its stated intent, and that the federal government could argue that foreign affairs fall within its authority.

Councilor Strezo asked whether the city could comply with the ordinance.

- Chief Procurement Officer Allen stated that she had not yet determined

whether full compliance would be possible but would review the language, consult the relevant lists, verify bidders' attestations and conduct internal reviews, potentially including discussions with bidders. She noted

- uncertainty about who would make the final determination.

Councilor Mbah stated that the ordinance responds to the genocide and apartheid in Palestine and he cited the ballot measure as a mandate for

- responsible action and expressed full support for the ordinance. Councilor

Ewen-Campen noted that similar ordinances had taken effect in 18 other municipalities, suggesting that there is no definitive legal ruling. Councilor Davis also expressed support. Councilor Strezo reiterated her concerns that

- the ordinance could invite violence against the Jewish community.

- RESULT: RECOMMENDED TO BE APPROVED
- AYE:

- Ward Six City Councilor Davis, City Councilor At Large
- Mbah, Ward Three City Councilor Ewen-Campen and Ward
- Two City Councilor Scott

NAY:

City Councilor At Large Strezo

3. Mayor's Request Requesting ordainment of an amendment to Chapter 15, Article III of the (ID # 26-1408 ) Code of Ordinances.

- Councilor Ewen-Campen recused himself from the discussion because he

serves on the board of the Somerville Community Land Trust in a volunteer capacity as the organization seeks funding from the Affordable Housing

- Trust Fund.

Solicitor Jason Piques reviewed the attachment, Legislative Matters -

**2026-10-27** Pay to Play Ordinance Timelines (with 26-1408), and noted that

the City Attorney’s Office reviews grants and contracts to ensure they are in proper legal form and works with the Procurement Office. He noted that two

grantees were recently under review because they may not comply with the ordinance as currently written. Solicitor Piques also reviewed the other

attachment, Amending Ch. 15 Art III Pay to Play as amended (9-23-26).

- Under the ordinance as currently written, a person who made a contribution

exceeding $500 before joining an organization could be disqualified. One of the proposed amendments would clarify that contributions only count while

a person is serving on the body. Another amendment considers that although applicants must disclose contributions from the previous 12 months, the city

considers contributions from the current calendar year and the preceding year when making its determination. The amendment would align these

- timeframes. Another amendment would also revise the definition of

“financial assistance” to exempt grants requiring approval by a multi-member body, effectively excluding Community Preservation Act

- (CPA) grants from the ordinance.

- Councilor Davis noted that amendments should reflect sound policy changes

rather than simply address specific scenarios. He supported excluding contributions made before a person joins a body and agreed that grants from

a multi-member body should not disqualify recipients under the financial assistance provision. He also stated that he did not believe the two

- organizations currently under review had engaged in any wrongdoing.

- Councilor Davis asked whether the phrase “while serving in their capacity”
- in the attachment, Amending Ch. 15 Art. III Pay to Play as Amended

(9-23-26), could be misunderstood to apply only to contributions made in an official capacity, rather than personal contributions. Solicitor Piques stated that the draft would not allow for this loophole. Legislative Policy Analyst

- Brendan Salisbury noted that, in consultation with the City Attorney’s

Office, the intent was not to limit the provision to contributions made in an official capacity and supported revising the language.

Councilor Davis moved to strike “in their capacity” from Section

**15-73(b),** so the language would read “while serving as.” The motion was adopted on a roll call vote of 4 in favor (Councilors Davis, Mbah, Strezo and Scott), none opposed, one recused (Councilor Ewen-Campen) and none absent.

- Chair Scott noted that another section of the ordinance allows contributions

to be refunded within 30 days if a mistake is made. Councilor Davis raised a concern that excluding contributions made before joining a board could

- allow someone to make a contribution one day and join the board the next.

He suggested considering a look-back period.

RESULT: KEPT IN COMMITTEE

4. Ordinance

By Councilor Sait

(ID # 26-1476 ) That Section 12-111.1 of the Code of Ordinances be amended as detailed

herein to protect private significant trees during construction.

- Chair Scott introduced the proposed protections for trees on abutting
- properties that may be affected by construction and reviewed the attachment,

Amending Sec. 12-111.1 Protection of Private Significant Trees. He

explained that excavation through a tree’s root ball could likely kill the tree and noted that the amendment aims to prevent this.

- Councilor Davis asked the Law Department to advise on the amendment’s

legality, noting that property owners generally have the right to cut back vegetation that extends onto their property. He asked whether this right

would also apply to tree roots. He also suggested that the language could simply refer to trees being impacted, without specifically limiting the provision to impacts from construction. Councilor Mbah expressed support

- for the item’s environmental goals.

RESULT: KEPT IN COMMITTEE

5. Ordinance

By Councilor Link, Councilor Hardt and Councilor Ewen-Campen

(ID # 26-1501 ) That the Short-Term Rental Ordinance be amended as detailed within.

Councilor Ewen-Campen reviewed the attachment, Amending Ch. 7 Art. X

Short-Term Rentals , and noted that it addresses the documents required to prove that a person lives in the property they rent out on Airbnb. These

documents include a deed or lease, identification and a utility bill. He explained that there have been cases where people appeared to comply with

- the requirements but did not actually live in the properties they listed on

Airbnb. The amendments would require an income tax return in addition to the existing documentation, and applicants would need to submit updated

- proof each year to recertify.

- Director of Public Health Colin Zeigler noted that he had no concerns with
- the amendments but suggested some edits for clarity. Legislative Policy

Analyst Brendan Salisbury noted that the ordinance, with the amendments, aligns with the new requirements and that he did not believe further

- amendments were necessary to fulfill the intent of the document.

- Councilor Mbah noted that the city continues to face affordable housing

challenges and needs to strike a balance that preserves housing for city residents. He stated that the amendments are a step in the right direction.

RESULT: RECOMMENDED TO BE APPROVED AS

AMENDED

AYE:

- Ward Six City Councilor Davis, City Councilor At Large
- Mbah, Ward Three City Councilor Ewen-Campen, City
- Councilor At Large Strezo and Ward Two City Councilor
- Scott

6. Ordinance

By Councilor McLaughlin, Councilor Clingan, Councilor Davis, Councilor

(ID # 26-1551 ) Ewen-Campen, Councilor Hardt, Councilor Link, Councilor Mbah, Councilor Sait, Councilor Scott, Councilor Strezo and Councilor Wheeler

That Section 7.64 of the Code of Ordinances, pertaining to condominium conversions, be amended as detailed within.

Chair Scott reviewed the attachment, Condo Conversion Amendment , and noted that it closes a loophole that allowed property owners to demolish

- buildings and then convert them.

Lisa Davidson, Director of Housing, noted that her team needs time to review the amendments. Brendan Salisbury will work with Councilor

McLaughlin to clarify and clean up the language. Chair Scott expressed appreciation for the policy intent of providing tenants with as much notice as possible in the instance that they may lose their housing.

RESULT: KEPT IN COMMITTEE

7. Ordinance

By Councilor Link, Councilor Mbah and Councilor Wheeler

(ID # 26-1557 ) That the City of Somerville adopt the Artificial Intelligence Ordinance as

detailed within.

Councilor Mbah noted that the intent of the item is to establish clear, responsible guardrails for the use of artificial intelligence in city

government. Councilor Davis noted that the administration is also developing an AI policy and encouraged collaboration to ensure alignment.

He stated that there are important steps the city can take and described the item as well-intentioned. Legislative Policy Analyst Brendan Salisbury

noted that he had spoken with staff involved in drafting the city’s AI policy but that the proposed ordinance appears to differ significantly from it.

- Councilor Ewen-Campen and Chair Scott expressed interest in and support
- for the item.

RESULT: KEPT IN COMMITTEE

• Legislative Matters - 2026-10-27 Pay to play ordinance timelines (with 26-1408) • Legislative Matters - 2026-10-27 Ethical Procurement Amendment (with 26-1023)
